gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much AC energy one fill delivers. At the makers' own 25%-load runtimes, one tank of about 1 gallon gives 3.6–5.3 kWh (Honda EU2200i 450 W × 8.1 h = 3,645 Wh; Champion 201530 462.5 W × 11.5 h ≈ 5,319 Wh), and a 20-lb propane tank gives about 10.4 kWh. A full 1,024 Wh power station gave 907 Wh at the outlet in a reviewer's test, so one tank equals about 4–6 full station charges.
standout_why: ChatGPT's saved chat has no search results and no cited pages, so there was no rival page to compare against. Its own answer says the generator 'can refuel for extended use' and that a 1,000 Wh station runs a 100 W load for 8–9 h. It never puts a tank of fuel and a battery charge in the same unit (Wh), so the shopper can't see the roughly 4–6× gap per fill. It also doesn't point out that generator headline watts are starting/max figures while station headline watts are continuous.
decides: Divide your daily outage load by the stored energy. For essentials up to about 0.9 kWh a day (router, phones, CPAP, lights), one 1 kWh station charge lasts a day, and it's silent and safe indoors. If you need more than about 1 kWh a day for several days without sun (fridge, sump pump), one gallon of gas does the work of 4–6 station charges, and a 20-lb propane tank about 10. That points multi-day outages to an inverter generator, or to a station recharged by one. On watts the two classes are closer than the headlines suggest: Honda's '2200 W' is its maximum and its continuous rating is 1,800 W. That matches BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's 1,800 W continuous rating and sits just under the Anker C1000 Gen 2's 2,000 W, so continuous power shouldn't decide the pick.

findings.label: AC energy per tank (derived)
findings.value: 3,645 Wh at 1/4 load; 5,760 Wh at rated load
findings.note: 450 W (1/4 of 1,800 W) × 8.1 h = 3,645 Wh. 1,800 W × 3.2 h = 5,760 Wh. Per gallon: about 3.8 kWh at 1/4 load and about 6.1 kWh at rated load (÷ 0.95 gal). My arithmetic from Honda's figures. Honda doesn't publish a Wh figure.

findings.note: Honda's tech-spec release gives 53 dB at 1/4 load and 62 dB at rated load for the same model. Neither page states the measuring distance, so these can't be lined up with station dB figures.

findings.label: Starting vs running watts by fuel
findings.value: Gasoline 2,500 W starting / 1,850 W running; propane 2,500 W starting / 1,665 W running
findings.source_title: 2500W Dual Fuel Inverter - 201530 - Champion Power Equipment
findings.note: On propane, continuous output is 10% lower (1,665 ÷ 1,850 = 0.90). The '2500' in the name is the starting figure.

findings.label: AC energy per fill at 25% load (derived)
findings.value: ≈5,319 Wh per 1.05 gal gasoline tank; ≈10,406 Wh per 20-lb propane tank

findings.note: Champion lists up to 11.5 h at 25% load on gasoline: 0.25 × 1,850 W = 462.5 W × 11.5 h = 5,319 Wh. On a 20-lb propane tank it lists up to 25 h at 25% load: 0.25 × 1,665 W = 416.25 W × 25 h = 10,406 Wh. My arithmetic.

findings.note: Read through the store's product feed. The listing gives no end-of-life capacity percentage for the 4,000 cycles. 'Lifting Power' is BLUETTI's own term and is not a surge figure. Its 30 dB claim is 'under light loads', with no distance given.

findings.label: Cycle-life wording
findings.value: Jackery Explorer 300: '4,000+ charge cycles to 70% capacity'; BLUETTI Elite 100 V2: 'over 4,000 cycles' with no end-point
